Pouvoir écouter ceux qui refusent le vac: Being able to listen to those who refuse the vaccine
Comme, des deux côtés, le dialogue n’exi: Because dialogue doesn’t exist on either side, La Converse tried to open it up to learn more.
A COVID-19 vaccination site. Photo: Pablo Ortiz
En pleine cinquième vague de la pandémie: In the middle of the fifth wave of the COVID-19 pandemic, attention is turning more than ever to those who are unvaccinated. This group, which makes up less than 15% of Quebec’s population, holds as many points of view as it has realities. Because dialogue doesn’t exist on either side, La Converse tried to open it up to learn more.
Voici ce que certains d’entre eux ont à: Here is what some of them have to say, and how experts respond. “I’m not anti-vaccine,” Emmanuel* says right off the bat. For this father, the problem is the imposition of the measure. “There are vaccines I’ve taken, others I haven’t, it’s still my choice,” he explains. As for the COVID-19 vaccine, it is its effectiveness that he questions and that led him not to get vaccinated. In his view, there is a lack of information about the vaccine. He fears in particular that receiving several vaccines for the same disease could weaken the immune system. A vaccine that is 90% effective would change his mind, he says, before adding that he distrusts the most recent vaccines. For example, under the best conditions, the flu vaccine <l1>prevents illness</l1> in 40% to 60% of the people who receive it.
Emmanuel appuie les mesures sanitaires c: Emmanuel supports public health measures such as physical distancing, mask wearing and handwashing. The Montréal resident says his decision is informed by the extensive research he does across a variety of sources: “I read the blogs of doctors who are for it, and of those who are against it.” He would like to see a greater diversity of viewpoints in the public sphere. “We hear the opinion of the doctors who are for vaccination, but not of those who are against. We always hear the government’s side, but not that of the people who are against it,” he laments. Ali*, who is in his mid-twenties, caught COVID-19 last spring. Fortunately, he recovered well. “The vaccine is experimental.
Je n’ai pas besoin de ce vaccin expérime: I don’t need this experimental vaccine that was rushed out in under a year. Even today, it’s still being refined,” says the man, who says he actively looks after his health through sports, healthy eating and spirituality. He compares the situation to other treatments. “The vaccines against measles, hepatitis or tetanus were developed over decades,” he points out, adding that he is apprehensive about the side effects of the immunization that COVID-19 vaccines provide. He is also concerned about pharmaceutical interests. “I look at both camps to get an idea of the situation. I don’t stay locked in conspiracy-theory thinking, but I doubt the opinions and recommendations of the so-called experts you see just about everywhere in the mainstream media,” he says. “As soon as you open your mouth and say you’re unvaccinated, you’re a conspiracy theorist,” sighs Marcelle*, a woman in her sixties.
Les tensions se font sentir au sein même: The tension is felt even within her own marriage, as her husband, who is vaccinated, laments her position. For her, pharmaceutical interests should be a warning sign, as should the alleged side effects of the vaccines. “I’m vaccinated myself, I had my daughters vaccinated against other diseases. I’m not someone who lives in conflict and protest,” she explains. Her position is based in particular on the statements of medical heavyweights who, in her view, have a lot to lose by speaking out against COVID-19 vaccines. The absence of diverse viewpoints leaves her perplexed. “Why don’t we take into account the opinion of those who disagree? Have we ever seen a debate here on TV where people say why they’re for and why they’re against?”
Ce qui la fera peut-être changer d’avis,: What might change her mind is a vaccine that targets the virus strain and doesn’t require multiple doses. It is an argument also made by Dr. Gary Kobinger, a specialist who co-invented the Ebola vaccine and who wants governments to look into studying a universal vaccine. A new vaccine that would take longer to develop, but would protect against the virus’s variants.
La chercheuse, professeure et pédo-psych: Cécile Rousseau, a researcher, professor, child psychiatrist and Canada Research Chair, has conducted extensive research on COVID-19. She has studied unvaccinated people in Quebec, but also in Ontario and Alberta. She points out that, in this debate, the two most antagonistic groups – the “antivax,” who see the vaccine as an assault or a weapon, and those who believe unvaccinated people are responsible for all our woes, and that they should be punished or denied care – are not so different from one another, a bit like a mirror effect. To address the doubts of Emmanuel, Ali and Marcelle, Dr. Rousseau offers the following explanations. “There are many infectious agents in our environments. The human body has the ability to defend itself against quite a few of them,” she reminds us. She gives the example of children, who are exposed to a large number of them, notably in daycare. They build up their defences as they go, so that they develop immunity and catch fewer and fewer illnesses. “Immunity is built from exposure to infectious agents that we are able to defeat.
Cependant, il y a certains agents infect: However, there are certain infectious agents that our bodies won’t be able to defeat,” adds the researcher, citing polio, tetanus and rabies. “Your immune system doesn’t get lazy when you’re given a vaccine. There is no competition between natural immunity and the immunity that vaccines provide,” the professor sums up. The mRNA vaccine used against the coronavirus that causes COVID-19 is relatively low-risk compared with other vaccines used in the past, including those against whooping cough and diphtheria. “There are relatively few side effects and less risk than with some other vaccines,” says the psychiatrist.
À tel point qu’on risque d’avoir une plu: So much so that you’re more likely to have a stronger reaction to a flu shot. Among the risks that have been identified are, for example, blood clots with AstraZeneca, or myocarditis and pericarditis. Alternatives exist for those at risk of suffering from these conditions. “The rates of side effects are not extraordinary, and in that case, the risk posed by the vaccine is lower than the risk posed by the coronavirus,” Dr. Rousseau sums up. It’s true that the COVID-19 vaccine was developed quickly. <l1>However, the mRNA technology that was used has been known and used since 1961</l1>. Given the urgency of the situation, thousands of teams worked on the problem, and data was collected by health systems around the world, which sped things up considerably. “What makes up for the speed of development is that we have far more data on the coronavirus vaccine than on vaccines whose development took decades, because it took more time to accumulate the same amount of data,” the researcher says. While clinical trials for other vaccines were conducted on thousands of people, millions of people have tested the COVID-19 vaccine. “Side effects occur either immediately or within four to six weeks of the vaccine – not after. What we know is that there won’t be any major problem with this vaccine,” says Dr. Rousseau.
« Les peurs individuelles, que ce soit p: “Individual fears, whether about health or a political and economic critique of science or pharmacology, are legitimate positions to question in a democracy, and entirely respectable,” believes Dr. Rousseau. The researcher goes on to say that it is justified to be critical of the health care system, science and pharmaceutical companies. “It’s true that the pharmaceutical industries are lining their pockets, that they are part of the multinational economy, that there are commercial interests,” she says.
Même chose pour le milieu scientifique,: The same goes for the scientific community, which doesn’t tell everything. “There have been a huge number of scientific scandals in recent decades, whether in the publication of results, bias, or commercial collusion. There are good reasons for people to have doubts and to say they don’t trust it. You have to understand that not every critical word about pharmaceutical lobbies, or about the way science announces and imposes itself, is a conspiracy theory,” she says. As part of her research, Dr. Rousseau looked at a sample of unvaccinated people in Canada. “It’s a very heterogeneous group, with a majority of people who have low social capital. So we’re talking about people who are in difficult economic conditions.”
Pourtant, ce ne sont pas elles qu’on ent: Yet they are not the ones we hear from when unvaccinated people are mentioned. The specialist also wishes that vaccinated people would not be presented as automatically in favour of vaccines. “What my research has shown is that not all vaccinated people are convinced of the merits of the vaccine. Ambivalence and criticism are just as present among the vaccinated. There are vaccinated people who are critical of the vaccine, and among the unvaccinated, others who are considering it.”
Cette ambivalence peut être liée à plusi: This ambivalence can be tied to several things, including a critical view of medicine or an alternative approach. Fear often shows up in people’s accounts. It can be linked to personal experiences with vaccines or with the health care system, as well as to the side effects of certain drugs or medical procedures. In addition, some people subscribe to an alternative approach to medicine – such as naturopathy, natural immunity, gentle medicine – or dread the invasive nature of medicine. An interest in alternative approaches to health is what motivated Adam*’s mother never to have him vaccinated. “Since I was born, I’ve never had a single vaccine,” says the man, now in his thirties, from his home in the Laurentians. “I remember my mother writing letters to the principal to keep us from getting vaccines. [...] She believed much more in natural and alternative medicine than in Western medicine,” he recalls. In his view, vaccinated people are more fragile, because their immune systems have been “compromised.” “For me, it’s better not to get vaccinated than to risk dying,” says the man, who prefers to look after his health with vitamins, healthy eating and physical activity.
« Que des gens ne puissent plus parler n: “That people can no longer speak or identify themselves [as unvaccinated] shows how far we’ve gone into something very unhealthy,” says A. Hadi Qaderi, a Montréal man in his fifties who has not been vaccinated. What he denounces is the social climate that public health measures have plunged us into: “It’s as if there were two camps demonizing each other. It comes through the government, the media and the scientific community. People who ask questions – which is the basis of science, after all – get called all sorts of things.” For Dr. Cécile Rousseau, “we have to remain credible and transparent in how we speak to the population, and remain credible to people who oppose public health measures and vaccination. The general idea is really to say: we’re going through a time of crisis, it’s important to mobilize together, but we have to be able to survive our disagreements.”
La Dre Isabelle Leblanc, médecin général: Dr. Isabelle Leblanc, a general practitioner in Côte-des-Neiges and president of the organization Médecins québécois pour le régime public, explains that she often sees patients who are less well informed. To counter the prevailing polarization, she advocates a human approach. “I sit down, I explain myself and I listen to their fears; it helps change minds,” she says. It doesn’t always work: some need several visits, and others still refuse. “Some of them cry because they’re glad we’re having an open discussion about it. People feel very judged, they’re scapegoats, so they can’t talk about it with their doctor for fear of being judged. We look at the reasons and we see how we can help them. People are glad we’re talking about it,” she concludes.
